Name: Adam
Transcript: Thanks for making the time. There are no right answers here, it is your experience I am after, and if you want to stop at any point just say. So, to begin. Can you tell me what it is like, sharing your home with a dog?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Erm. That is a big question, isn't it. I suppose she is just there. That is the first thing. Bramble is just there, all the time. I come down in the morning and she is sat on the second stair, because she is not allowed past the second stair, and she has got her chin on her paws, waiting. And I have not even got my eyes properly open and something in me has already gone soft. I do not know how else to put it. The house is never empty now. Even when it is quiet it is not empty.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You said something in you has already gone soft. What is that like?

Name: Juno
Transcript: It is like being caught. I am not a soppy person, or I did not think I was. I was the one who said no dog, for about four years I said no dog, absolutely not, I know who ends up walking it. And now I am stood in the hall at half six in my dressing gown having a full conversation with an animal. She does this stretch, the long one, front legs right out, and she groans all the way through it. And I have started groaning back at her. That is the state of me now.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You said you were the one who said no dog. How did that change?

Name: Juno
Transcript: My partner wore me down, that is the short version. There was a website, and a photograph of her stood in a yard looking absolutely miserable and the wrong side of thin, and once you have seen a photograph like that you have already lost the argument, you just have not admitted it yet. I kept saying all the sensible things right up until the day we went to meet her. And then she leant on my legs in that yard, the same lean she does now at the door, inside about ninety seconds of meeting me. And that was that. I did not stand a chance. I still say I was talked into her, and my partner still says I was the one who filled the form in, and we are both right.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Take me through an ordinary morning. What actually happens?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Right. So the alarm goes at twenty past six. And straight away there is the question of who gets up, which is the first thing that happens in our house every single day, and it is not always friendly. My partner says they did it yesterday. I say they did not, they did it the day before. And Bramble hears the alarm and she starts up, not barking, more of a, a sort of whine that she can keep going for a very long time without seeming to breathe. And whoever cracks first gets up. I crack first. I am not proud of it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What is that like, being the one who cracks first?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Annoying. No, it is more than annoying. There is a bit of me stood at the top of the stairs thinking, right, so that is settled then, I am the one who does this, for ever. And it is not the twelve minutes. It is what the twelve minutes says. That I will always go. That they know I will always go, and so they can lie there and let me. And then I am at the bottom and she is so pleased, she does the whole body wag, the back half going one way and the front half the other, and the annoyance just goes. Which is its own annoying thing, because I would quite like to stay cross.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You would like to stay cross.

Name: Juno
Transcript: I would. Because then I could have it out properly, at a reasonable hour, and get somewhere with it. But you cannot carry a mood down those stairs. She takes it off you at the bottom. And then we are out of the door, and by the time we are back I have forgotten what I was going to say, or it has gone small. So it never gets said. Five years of it never getting said.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And the walk itself. What happens on that walk?

Name: Juno
Transcript: It is the same walk. Out of the door, left, down past the allotments, round the bottom field and back up the lane. Forty minutes. She knows every inch of it, she could do it without me, and there are mornings where I genuinely think she is walking me. There is a gap in the hedge at the bottom where she always stops and puts her whole head in, every morning, the same gap, and there has never been anything in it. Not once. Five years and that hedge has never once produced a single thing. But she has to check.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What is that bit of the walk like for you?

Name: Juno
Transcript: I love it. I did not expect to hear myself say that. The first year I resented it, I really did, I thought, this is forty minutes I have not got. And now it is the bit of the day that is mine. Nobody can ask me for anything, because I am out with the dog, and that is a completely respectable reason to be unavailable. Nobody argues with it. And my head goes quiet on that lane in a way it does not anywhere else. Not because I am thinking things through. I am mostly watching her nose.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Watching her nose.

Name: Juno
Transcript: Yes. It sounds ridiculous said out loud. But there is something about how much she is enjoying it. She is having the time of her life in a wet hedge, at ten past seven, in February. Every morning. And you cannot stand next to that much enthusiasm for a hedge and stay in a bad mood, it is not possible. It is a bit like being with a small child, except she is not going to grow out of it and start being embarrassed by me.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Does she go off the lead down there?

Name: Juno
Transcript: On the bottom field, yes. She is a lurcher, so there is always a risk. If something moves she is gone, and there is no recall in the world that will hold her once she has gone. I have watched her go across that field after a hare and it is one of the best things I have ever seen, and I am furious the entire time it is happening. And then she comes back grinning, tongue out, absolutely delighted with herself, and I am stood at the gate having aged about four years. And I still let her off. Every single morning I stand there and weigh it up, and every single morning I let her off, because the look on her at full stretch is worth more to me than the twenty minutes of worry.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You mentioned resenting it, that first year. Can you say more about that?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Erm. Yes. The first year was hard. I had not reckoned on how much of my time stopped being mine. It was not the money, although there is that, the money is not nothing. It was that you cannot just go. We used to go off for a weekend with about an hour's notice, and now there is a whole logistics operation. Who has her, what does she need, is my mum free that weekend, is the kennels any good, will she settle. And there was a stretch, maybe six months in, where I thought, I have made a mistake here. I did not say that out loud to anybody.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What stopped you saying it out loud?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Because it is a terrible thing to say, isn't it. She is a rescue. She had a rough time of it before us, you can still see it in her, she flinches if you move your arm too fast above her head, even now. And I am going to sit at a table and say I regret her. No. So I did not say it, and then it went away, mostly, the way things do. But I would be lying if I told you it never comes back. It comes back on a Sunday night in February when it is chucking it down and she still needs going out at ten o'clock.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Tell me about one of those nights.

Name: Juno
Transcript: There was one. It was proper rain, the sideways sort, and I had a cold coming, and I stood in the porch with her lead in my hand for a good two minutes just looking at the door. Not moving. And she was sat behind me, completely still, not pushing at me, not doing the whine, just waiting to see what I decided. That is the bit that got me, actually. She was not begging. She was just waiting. So I put my coat on and we went out. And we got about as far as the postbox and we both turned round at the same second, without either of us deciding it, and came home. And we stood in the kitchen dripping on the floor and I gave her a rub with the towel, and I felt closer to her than I have on any of the nice walks.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was it about that night that made you feel closer?

Name: Juno
Transcript: I think because it cost me something. That sounds a bit grand. But the easy days do not prove anything, do they. Anybody can walk a dog in June. That night I did not want to, and she knew I did not want to, I am sure of that, and we went anyway. And then we both gave up at exactly the same moment, which felt like an agreement rather than a failure. Like we had negotiated it stood there by the postbox. And I got something out of that night I would not have got if the weather had been fine.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You used the word agreement. What does an agreement look like, between you and Bramble?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Well, she has not signed anything. Erm. It is more that we have worked out what we each do. She does not go past the second stair. I do the mornings, mostly. She knows the sound of the drawer the lead is in, and she does not get up until she hears it, because she has learnt that getting up early does not make it happen any faster. There are rules in that house and neither of us wrote them down. That is a strange thing to have with another creature, when you stop and think about it. We have never once had a conversation and we both know exactly where we stand.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And coming home. What is that like?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Oh, it is the best bit of the day, without question. You hear her before you see her, the claws going on the floor in the hall, and she cannot get to the door fast enough, she actually skids into it. And then she does not jump up, she has never been a jumper, she leans. She puts her whole weight against your legs and stands there with her head down. And then she has to go and fetch the rabbit, this toy with no ears left on it, and bring it to you, every single time, and she cannot carry it and whine at the same time so it all comes out muffled through the rabbit.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What is that like to walk into?

Name: Juno
Transcript: It is being wanted. Plainly. Nobody else in my life is that pleased to see me, and I say that with no bitterness at all, it is just a fact. My partner says hello from the other room, and that is fine, that is what adults do, I do the same. But she stops everything. Whatever she was doing, and she was doing something, she was asleep in the good chair that she is not allowed in, all of it stops the second the key goes in the door. I have never had a welcome like that off anything in my life.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Does that change anything, having a welcome like that every day?

Name: Juno
Transcript: I think it makes me come home. There was a stretch where I would find reasons to stay out, nothing dramatic, just one more thing to sort out before I left. And now there is a clock on me. Not a guilty clock exactly, she is asleep, she is fine, she does not know what time it is. But I want the door bit. So I come home. My partner has noticed that.

Name: Adam
Transcript: How do you know they have noticed?

Name: Juno
Transcript: They said it once, in passing. Something like, you are back early for a Thursday. And they were pleased, I think, they meant it nicely. But there was something else in it as well, which was, you will come home for the dog. And I did not know what to do with that. Because it is true. I am not going to sit here and pretend it is not true.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was it like, hearing that?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Uncomfortable. But not in a way I could argue with, which is worse. I have thought about it a lot since. The dog is easier. That is the thing I keep landing on and then moving off, because it is not a nice thing to think about yourself. She does not need me to have got anything right. She has no memory of what I said last Tuesday, or what I did not say. Whereas with a person you walk in and whatever was going on before is still going on, it is stood there waiting for you in the hall as well. So of course I come home for the dog. Who would not.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You said you land on it and then move off it.

Name: Juno
Transcript: Yes. Because I do not know what to do with it. Either it means she has been very good for us, because we both love her and we talk about her and we laugh at her, and we do, we have got about forty stupid voices for her now. Or it means we have found something to talk about instead of talking. And I genuinely do not know which one it is. Some weeks it is obviously the first. Some weeks I am not so sure. I have not got to the bottom of it and I am not certain I want to, if I am honest with you.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Mm. Can I ask about a time when she has been unwell?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Yes. So in the spring she came up lame on a Saturday. Back leg, not putting any weight on it at all, holding it right up off the ground. And she is a lurcher, she is all leg, so a back leg is not nothing on her. And I had this, it went straight to the worst thing. I had her in the car inside about four minutes. And the whole way there I was doing the sums in my head, what do we do, what if it is the thing that it is at her age.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was happening in you, on that drive?

Name: Juno
Transcript: My hands were shaking on the wheel, which surprised me. I am usually all right in an emergency, I am the one people ring. And I could hear myself talking to her in the back in a voice I did not recognise. Very bright, very calm, telling her it was fine and we would be there in a minute. And she was completely silent, which she never is in the car, and that made it worse, because I thought, she knows. And underneath all of it there was this other thing going on, which was, when did I let something matter this much. When did that happen.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And at the vet?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Well. It was a thorn. A blackthorn, right up in the pad, you could not see it at all until they shaved her foot. Fifteen minutes and forty quid and she walked out of there like nothing had happened, dragging me across the car park. And I sat in the car afterwards and cried, which I had not done in the waiting room, I saved that up for the car park. Relief, obviously. But also something else that I would not quite call embarrassment. Shock, maybe. At the size of what I had felt on the way there.

Name: Adam
Transcript: The size of what you had felt.

Name: Juno
Transcript: It was out of proportion. That is what I mean by it. She had a thorn in her foot and I had spent twenty minutes organising my own grief in advance, in traffic. And what that told me is that it is coming. Not that day, but it is coming, because she is six and lurchers are not a forty year proposition, are they. So that Saturday was a rehearsal. And I did not enjoy finding out that I have got the whole thing ready to go.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is that something you have thought about since?

Name: Juno
Transcript: I try not to. I am aware that is not much of an answer. It sits there. When she is asleep on her side doing the running legs, the dreaming, sometimes I watch her and I think, right, I am going to have to do this properly one day and I have no idea at all how I will be. And then I stop myself, because she is asleep on a rug and she is absolutely fine, and it is a waste of a Tuesday evening to sit there grieving a dog who is snoring at you.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Yeah. Can we go somewhere lighter for a minute. You mentioned the groomer.

Name: Juno
Transcript: Oh, the groomer. Yes. So she goes every couple of months. She does not need much doing, she is short coated, but she gets a wash and her nails done, because I cannot do her nails, she will not have it, she takes her foot away and looks at me like I have suggested something disgusting. And I drop her off and then I have got two hours.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And what happens in those two hours?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Nothing. That is the honest answer. The first time I thought, brilliant, two hours, I will get so much done. And I came back into the house and stood in the kitchen and did not know what to do with myself. It was so quiet. And it was not a nice quiet, it was a wrong quiet, like when the fridge stops humming and you suddenly notice a noise you did not know you had been hearing. I kept looking at the second stair. I think I made a cup of tea and sat down and looked at my phone for an hour and a half.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was that quiet like?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Er. It was like the house was on standby. Everything in it is arranged around her now, and we never sat down and decided to arrange it. There is a bed under the window because that is where the sun comes in at eleven. The good chair has a blanket over it because of her, even though she is not allowed on it, which tells you how that rule is going. Her lead is on the third hook. And with her not in it the whole place was just a set. Furniture waiting for somebody.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Furniture waiting for somebody.

Name: Juno
Transcript: Yes. And I did not like it at all. I was quite relieved when the two hours were up, and I went and got her twenty minutes early and had to stand outside on the pavement. And she came out smelling of something floral and looking, frankly, appalled about it, and the house was fine again the minute she was back in it. It is a bit alarming, that, when you say it out loud to somebody. That a whole house can go on standby waiting for a dog.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What is alarming about it?

Name: Juno
Transcript: I suppose because of how much is resting on her. If a house can go flat for two hours, what happens when it is not two hours. That is the thought I do not let myself finish. And it is a lot to hang on an animal who cannot be told any of it. She does not know she is doing it. She is just lying in the sun at eleven because the sun is there at eleven.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Mm. You said earlier that you both laugh at her, you and your partner.

Name: Juno
Transcript: We do. Constantly. We have got voices for her, we do her internal monologue, which is mostly complaints about the pair of us and the standard of service. It is genuinely the funniest thing in that house. And I do think that is real, that is not us avoiding anything, that is just a good thing we have got hold of. But I have noticed we do it at about the point in the evening where we might otherwise be talking about something else. Half nine. That is when the dog voices come out.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What might you otherwise be talking about at half nine?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Money. The fact that neither of us has said anything at all about next year. My mum, who is not well, and who neither of us wants to start on at half nine. There is a list. There is always a list, everybody has got one, I am not claiming that is unusual. But the dog is a very good door to close on it. She comes and puts her chin on your knee at about that time, and it is completely legitimate to stop talking and make a fuss of her instead.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And how is that, the door closing?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Two ways at once, which is what I keep saying to you, I know. Relieved, because I do not want to do the list at half nine either. And then a bit uneasy, because being relieved is a sign of something, isn't it. If I am that glad of the interruption. But then I think, she is also the reason we are in the same room at all. Before her we would be on separate floors doing separate things and calling it an evening. Now we are both on the sofa with a dog laid between us, which is more than a lot of people manage. So which is it. I do not know which it is.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You do not have to resolve it for me.

Name: Juno
Transcript: Good, because I cannot. I have been round and round it. It is one of those things where the answer changes depending on the week I have had.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And at the end of the day, where does she sleep?

Name: Juno
Transcript: In the kitchen. That was the rule and the rule has held, more or less. She has a bed in there with a blanket on it that used to be mine. And the last thing that happens every night is that I go in and say goodnight to her, out loud, like she is a person, and she does not get up, she just thumps her tail twice on the bed. Twice. Never three times. And I put the light off and go up. It is the most ridiculous ritual and if I ever skipped it I think I would lie there upstairs thinking about it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there anything about living with her that you have not been able to say to anybody?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Erm. Probably the regret, from that first year. I have never said that to my partner. Not once, not even as a joke. And she has been with us five years now, so it is a bit late to be bringing it up at the table. And maybe the other one, which is that I know I am kinder to her than I am to the people in my house. I am endlessly patient with a dog who has eaten a sock. Somebody leaves a cupboard door open and I am not patient at all. I do not know what to do about that, but I do know it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What is it like to say that here?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Fine, actually. Easier than I thought it would be. It is not really a confession, is it, it is just how it is. I think most people with a dog would tell you something similar if you gave them twenty five minutes and nobody they lived with was listening.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there anything else about living with her that we have not touched on?

Name: Juno
Transcript: Erm. Only that it is very ordinary. That is the thing I would want to get across, if it is any use to you. None of this is dramatic. It is a lot of standing in a wet field holding a bag. It is hoovering hair off a sofa twice a week and finding it on your coat anyway. And somewhere in all that ordinary stuff she has got herself right into the middle of the house, and I could not tell you which day that happened. There was no day. It is just that now, if you asked me to describe home, she would be in the description and I would not have to think about it first.

Name: Adam
Transcript: That is really helpful. Thank you. I will stop the recording there.
